i wanted to love this film, i went in to the theatres and through the extreme sensory overload of the imax format and the music stabbing my ears, i came out with my mouth wide agape - going wow, this sure was great and it was in so many ways. i am no expert in greek literature but i know about the odyssey and went back and visited a lot of those and felt more appreciation for the film. i loved the choices nolan had made in adapting it, i loved the theological impact of this reinterpretation, loved the cersie reinterpretation from a seductress, loved the anti-war stance it was trying to take with the falling of troy, the sheer audacity of the film, the craft and the way the world was built with painstaking detail, the actors all do a fantastic job [hathway and pattinson cant stop winning], nolan felt like a bard for a civilisation at dusk (iykwim) and yet i dont love the film and nolan is to be blamed for that

when my ears stopped ringing and my adrenaline from the bollywood esque climax fight got down, i thought and thought some more and as the fog faded, as the sirens got less loud, i stood in front of a large lake looking onto the reflection of the film and it was a mere illusion

nolan with all he has done and all the great choices he has made in adapting wants to not spend a second in breathing and instead wants suffocating bombardment all the time. even the moments that deserve some stillness, it feels like he is paranoid that the audience might be breathing for a second. odysseus meeting penelope is supposed to be this incredibly cathartic, devastating, beautiful moment and its written and performed amazingly but the way its cut makes it feel like a mr beast video more than it does a culmination of the titular journey. i remember the films in flashes and fleeting images akin to having dreamed of watching the film. there are beautiful shots, that must have been a painstaking effort to take, that if you blink you will miss, there for 3 seconds. this also makes the characters feel shallow and lackluster, i don’t flinch when telemachus is in danger or about to die or when he reunites with his father, i dont flinch when any of his crewmates are dying because they are all fodder. fodder to the larger action machine that wants to keep chugging to maximize efficiency. athena is barely there, barely talking, talking only in brooding exposition, dumbed down to a level of bafflement. the things i praised it for are things that seem incredible on paper and seem incredible when told but somehow they lack the ingenuity when seen

this is a film i really want to love and i so wish i could love this film, i want to with every fiber in my being but it doesnt let me

remnants of a more hopeful india where these projects were explored for the sake of an anthropological survey - funded by the government

regardless, exceptionally fascinating that they woke up one day and they are administered by the british government/indian government or whoever else. their island arbitrarily shifts "ownership" without them knowing.

why are they so hostile to outsiders? why do they spray arrows at any bystander? or kill the christian missionary who landed upon their home uninvited? well, because the last time they opened up their lands to an outsider was Maurice Vidal Portman, the british naval officer who kidnapped 6 of them when they welcomed him. 4 of them died in captivity when they contracted diseases that they didnt have immunity to, they were forced to pose next to him as he fancied himself a "father of the andaman" and then the 2 were returned as they barely survived the infection with toys, utensils as peace offerings. it is highly probable that an untold number of sentinelese died from an epidemic triggered by the children's return. not once but multiple times he did this - through the late 80s. he essentially treated the indigenous people as semi-domesticated pets, forcing them to live in a state of controlled captivity while completely ignoring the deadly impact that British diseases, alcohol, and lifestyle changes were having on their populations - and also, ofc morality of it all - for his colonial mind, it was just more things to colonize. portman took thousands of photographs of the islanders. he forced them into rigid, uncomfortable poses to capture what he considered "authentic" or "savage" behavior. because the sentinelese quickly learned to hide whenever his ships approached, portman’s shore parties would raid their empty villages, ransacking their huts and stealing their weapons, tools, and personal belongings for his collection. he also had a homo-erotic fascination with the young men he would kidnap from the various tribes as evident from the photos. by the time portman retired, the british had decimated the broader great andamanese population from an estimated ~5k-6k people down to just a few hundreds.

british colonial conquest (as most colonizers) has caused pain and death across the world and the sentinelese are a small remnant of what they left in their wake

reviews.review:
big kitties or how tough it is to write contemporary social satire

i feel like it’s one of the most daunting things to set a film in reality and a present times milieu and do a social satire without being overly didactic and seem like you’re hitting the audiences with a brick over and over again 

what works great is allegorical satire - say star wars with its vietnam war roots. at the same time, a present time realistic satire needs to have something to create mystique or else it would be boring as fuck. adam mckay does it with a meteor, lynch does it with surreal abstract creatures, this film choses a man travelling from the future to save us from the AI singularity. god i wish i never start on a film like this

this is ‘let people enjoy things’ the finale - the future we all seem to be heading towards. granted the future wont be a wasteland that snows all the time but rather a more bleaker post apocalyptic scenario.

the film is trying to tell us a lot of things about the hypnosis our devices have on us but it does falter to the oh so common talking down trap that a lot of films do. dumb teenagers becoming zombies with phones gets tiring 3 seconds in because its not the relationship most genz have with their phones. everyone i know wants to shoot the piece of brick that is their phone but can’t - some more empathy would have been nice but i understand the film can only do so much especially when most of it is trying to show us the post-truth world we are inhabiting

relationships ARE being destroyed by VR or AI psychosis. just a few weeks ago, 4o was shut down leading to a lot of people’s AI romantic partners disappearing causing complete and utter meltdown. its easier to entrain ourselves than ever and easier to forego any semblance of struggle because well sedation is just cheaper and easier especially considering capitalism has nothing for you, wealth has been hoarded. the scarcity is what creates value for most assets in the word. 

this is something i wish the film spent some more time on. i wish the implication wouldn’t simply be pizza guy dumb and wants to live in a fantasy land but rather pizza guy is systematically exploited causing him to seek refuge in fantasy and virtual reality. there are more interesting conversations to he had along these lines and would have had the film feel so much more richer.

the way the film chooses to introduce its characters with the temporal shifts is nice but the film really doesnt connect any characters that much deeply until ingrid’s story. the film really doesnt grip until they are near the boy’s house. post which the film really takes shape because the satire becomes more animated and film also has some really fun sequences which make the film… fun. 

i loved the incredibly dramatic pre-finale, the faux ending and the real ending.

the film couldn’t have had a happy ending in any shape way or form because we aren’t getting one either. the titular phrase is what we shall be left with. a bleak post apocalyptic world we are already in which won’t have any obvious telltale signs for when you will know to revolt or be alarmed, it will be subtle and it will be too late until you realize.

what was it all about, anyway?

dhurandhar is fun in the way it is executing itself. there is incredible action, fun dialogues, some incredibly star backed swooning moments. this is all i want from a well made bollywood film and this is all there! there is a great soundtrack, fun visuals and a super entertaining flow that the 3.5 hours runtime breezes through

but, this is it. i dont love the film at all and thats mainly because of how confusing it is in what it is

is it a true story being retold of a brave spy? it’s not because this spy never existed. the gangs and their wars are absolutely true but the spy wasn’t there

was this spy an excuse to get to make a film about karachi gang wars? maybe. is this why ranveer singh is a plastic doll throughout the film with no character? maybe

why is ajit doval portrayed as a bumbling idiot waiting for “a better government”? 

why is there an insertion of live 26/11 captured audio even though it’s all fabricated and the story isn’t served at all through it? why are we reminded of the pain just before we get cool hanumankind rap and boom bap cool guy action? 

it’s a very competently made confused film - but fun regardless i guess

also, i wish we have such nice unfiltered treatment of adults and such subject matters. its okay if not every film has to cater to eventual TV licensing and runs

the film i make after i have a fight with my mom

what a fun film that has so much going for it and is so brilliant at a lot of places. i want more films like these in indian cinema, more genre fun pretty please

that being said, there is so much that just leaves me like :( because so much could have been that isn’t. one thing that turned me off to everything (which took rajit kapoor to turn me on again) was the post modernist millennial humor. i dont usually have such a reaction usually but oh my god the “cliche” dialogue made me want to kill myself. i would implore people to not do such mega vivid in your face millenial humor for the potential laughs you might get out of your friends because it takes the audience out so massively from this beautiful world youre creating. it is sometimes okay if your world is tense and feels like so for a while - witty jokes aren’t required at every running second of a murder investigation especially since they don’t weave themselves into situations or the negotiations but rather ram their ugly rear alike marvel one liners

that being said, such a well made film! everyone gives such a great performance. some great moments especially their fight but one thing is a huge letdown is the way the mother-son dynamic exploration is severely limited? this might sound crazy given there is this greatly explosive scene between them (which i loved) but i would want to feel empathy towards both or either or connect in a way which is not purely well-framed expository explosions. 

i love u rajit kapoor! i will move mountains for u <3

very torn on this one. there are so many things which appeal to me and so many that i have an ambiguous stance on 

there is a real story to be told which is necessary about sexual repression amongst indian men which often exasperates itself when there is an attached component of closely knit close quarters nuclear families and a general sense of insecurity amongst them

extramarital affairs, land disputes, internal quarrels about ambitions - this is the story of every indian household (barring upper middle classes) and what fascinates me a lot is the way kanu ties it to the sexuality of guru

there is a coming of age story wrapped somewhere within where he comes of age when he cums. if you will entertain my abrasive language for a while, a big part of the second half treads towards guru finding solace with the other ladies confronting. 

what i guess leaves me torn is that are we to believe the pent up sexuality lent itself to his deliriums solely - and if yes, then is the unresolved trauma from his father not a major component in his life anymore? maybe its the love he gets from priti which sort of brings the much needed balance in his life? 

regardless of this i am happy to be able to see this in the theatres! i had to go to chembur to catch it but hey atleast its here! hope everyone keeps making offbeat wacky flicks like these. love u kanu <3

neeraj ghaywan fair and squarely puts his gaze at something that our cinema sort of pretends never happened - lockdown and the mismanagement. there are a few “alt” voices like sinha’s bheed that come close to it but while bheed seems more interested in dissecting the logistics, the mismanagement and the failures from a more farther placed lens - neeraj zooms into people

foregoing the pandemic and the titular problem, there are a lot of other trimmings here that ensure the milieu isn’t only plot-forward but rather deeply human. this tense foreboding feeling of utter disrespect and second-guessing that ensues when you’re a marginalised person in our country, in the supposed “modern age” isn’t anything short of devastating - i have talked about this at length but i shall mention it anytime i get. beneath the glimmering “smart cities” lie systematically segregated people in 2025

over and all, incredible. everyone is incredible and at their top. super inspiring. super jealous.

there are some trimmings of misogyny (often subtextual) which is purely limited to the degenerate characters and not the whole film’s collective humor sense. 

its fun, its beautiful, its funny, its engaging. i love this film

but sadly, for me, thats all it invokes. i can look at it, appreciate the technicalities but there is an absolute numbness that comes over me as i do that

before i came to the review section or looked up anything about the film, i knew this wouldn't be positively received or have universal acclaim because the film is clearly very intentionally divisive and polarizing

for me, this might be one of ari aster's best because the dread is so uniformly dispersed amongst other black comedy elements that makes the whole thing so goddamn entertaining. there is this almost mechanical stochastic distribution of the dread that it is never overpowering and never underdelivering either

the crux being the issue at hand, in the small sleepy town of eddington, built on nearby reclaimed native land and how covid sort of spirals everything [and there is this datacenter that is used as a plot at several stages]

going into the film excepting some neatly tied message and clear "siding" would be a mistake because then this would undermine the whole film and the milieu it's so carefully setting up. doing a "wow look at these maga idiots and liberals are good" would undermine the entire thematic cohesion

the film ruffles feathers because it also shows the youth caring about BLM and all the right causes, but you also get to witness the performative-ness associated with these causes. there are people who merely posture, there are people who merely pretend to have empathy. and it's okay to show them as is. it doesn't delegitimize or digs on the people doing the activism. it shows the underlying racial biases as much as it shows the "i don't see color" people. truth being they exist amongst us, whether we like it or not. conspiracy rabbit holes are real, whether we like it or not. a lot of people on the internet prey on the trauma you carry, whether we like it or not. sadness and anger in everyone in the train or in the streets, whether we like it or not.

post 2020, we have been deeply polarized. we are fucked. spiritually and cohesively. i am not on no dramatic shit either, there is a general sense of dread everyone simmers in. this dread is captured in the film.

the dream is conveyed from the utter loneliness and ennui felt by the "distancing" or how the music shifts from one fit for a western to music fit for... well, hereditary.

there is a lot to love about this film and a lot to enjoy but for me the ultimate thing the film wants to scream at you is that hey you guys can lose arms, be blown up, get paralyzed, do your little culture wars but remember what shall prevail? capitalism! and sam altman's massive datacenters!

adapting a piece of art is often an obtuse task and doing that with dostoevsky and his often large books and converting that into a bollywood musical while starring the golden boy raj kapoor as the lead actor in it playing raskolnikov and through all this getting an incredible film made is a task in the purest form of the word

the film transforms st. petersburg of 1860s into 1950s bombay (then, not part of maharashtra and not called mumbai either). there are several very faithful adaptations and portrayals like Marmeladov and Katerina but what's far more interesting to me are the characters which weren't completely faithful to the book

indian subcontinent is wildly different from our western counterparts. our sentiments and sensibilities have evolved into this weird mixture of british-era "royalty" puritanical beliefs alongside with some remnants of our pre-colonization traditions remaining. what this essentially does is create this environment of utter disdain and lack of empathy towards anything that hasn't fit our mould. we see this in how anything sexual is considered outright vulgar and a disgrace in our country, anything romantic [even cupping hands with your partner] is a symbol of corruption and people are in 2025 regularly beaten up if they are seen kissing in public. this creates a cocktail where society is very rigid and isn't forgiving. why this tangent? well, because this lends us some perspective of why you couldn't directly lift the characters as is from the book

sonya could not have been a prostitute ever in the book because the collective society would not have accepted even a slight implication that "these people" make up the fabric of our society just as much as everyone else and hence deserve the same empathy when they suffer through something. this is why, through the poverty and through everything, she is not a sex worker but instead does tailoring for some lecherous men. soni instead is a victim of poverty and the preying that she is done on by the most affluent men because of her poverty

"gareeb ladki ko bhains bakri ki tarah khareedne waala dhanshah sharif aur mai mujrim?"

similarly,
raskolnikov couldn't have murdered the old lady with an axe - our society knows one thing which is that collectively violence against women is the hallmark of a villain. no matter the circumstances, no matter the situation [this might also stem from the lack of equality between men and women further exasperating this visceral reaction between the murder of each but I digress]. so, instead its a sly pawnbroker. a pawnbroker that is a representation of the capitalist overlords but in a microcosm.

raj kapoor does an incredible job as ram mehra aka raskolnikov. and puts to rest all and each implications that he can only do charlie chaplinesque roles

and finally, this all makes the film into this beautiful concoction that not only manages to adapt an incredible book into this brevity exercise [omitting raskol's family for this] but also a poignant criticism of capitalism to its fullest. addressing socio-economic disparities in 1958 with one of the biggest stars being the proponent for it.

"ye mera karam hai? mai tumhe bataata hu. chalak logo ne apne aisho aaramo ke liye duniya bhar ka dhan ikhatta kar liya aur lakho croro ko gareeb kar diya. mera jurm gareeb hona hai."

absolute cinema

there is an experience that you can have if you're indian that is NOT possible anywhere else in this whole world. go find a local theatre frequented by the average person - don't go to pvr icon in andheri or palladium in lower parel to watch this for example. watch in a theatre frequented by people - average people.

what you will end up seeing is this realtime metamorphosis where in when the film begins, the people in audience are there laughing at the specially abled as is the trope in bollywood. some of them don't but most do because we have been fed this as a trope since forever. however, this film does something so beautifully which is play into that. watch that laughter turn into not laughing at them but rather laughing with them and its beautiful. a realtime transformation of people into having empathy for a large set of people because a star had a big name film to portray that.

it's cheesy, full of tropes [side plots are boring and for gags] and yet has its heart in the right place and is actually impactful.

there is this palpable tension that precedes every major final destination trademark scene - this beat by beat chain of events that is foreboding in a way that is bound to leave you anxious and the film never falters even once on delivering those

the film is so incredibly charming and such a thrill ride in every sense of the word. what really is the most charming quality of the film is this irreverence it has - this spitting on hubris manifest that humans tend to carry in the face of something inevitable and inescapable which is death. i love the treating of every character and person as this puny being who is unable to control a single aspect of their life. this sense of nihilism actually evokes a deep resilience and speaks to something deeper - there are two options, either to lock yourself in a cabin or to just live your life and get crushed by a boulder if push comes to shove

death is seen as this ominous entity, personified by wind chimes and accidental falling of objects. the soundtrack accentuating the trivial and intrinsically transitive nature of human beings.

loved it so much

"the oil is treacherous because it's trying to disguise itself as water"

lessons of darkness is one of those works which touches something so innate yet indescribable nerve within us - it's a work that leaves reverberations echoing across several kilometers - a work that carries this je ne sais quio quality within itself that it undoubtedly juxtaposes this beautiful orchestral dreamscape with the hellscape which is our earth and the things that we are doing to it

there are no shortage of documentaries and great documentaries with tons of verbage helping us get to the root of several issues - often doctored, stiched together in a way that makes sense. presented in a way no different than fiction - in which the story is told by the makers more so than the people being featured in the documentary (its treacherous in this manner ;) ) but regardless a work like this, a work devoid of commentaries or dialogues or carefully placed expositions and contextual clues is so riveting.

the film makes you weep and feel scared to your core. it titilates you in a way that few others do and all while by just showing the imagery. it shows you the way we collectively have made our nurturing grounds spit out hellish fires. shows us the human tendency to conquer every inch while "taming" every element. while there are a few humans who weep in this, the one who weeps the utmost remains to be our earth - crying and letting out nightmarish firey tears - you can almost hear her screaming if you listen closely enough

do not give up your music, don’t put down the guitar! 

an incredibly fun allegorical historical drama piece that wants to say a lot of and does - wants to show a lot and does - all while making sure the package is as entertaining as it comes

gentrification and appropriation - in modern leftist liberal circles, there are several conversations about this but yet there is rarely a meaningful resolution to it all. partly because capitalism by it’s very form seeks to commodify every entity that exists in the slightest - gentrification and appropriation is beneficial to capitalism and the upholders of capitalism. who are the upholders and first-row beneficiaries of the capital? its white people. and they have been so historically. and yet, by its very nature - by its very form - by its very core / capitalism cannot create culture or foster it. cant create soul and movement. it can only seek to replicate and imitate. partly also because they don’t feel the need to - not much different from the tech bros (who are the zeitgeist klanmans) espousing takes such as ai will replace art and swinging around their ai slop seeking to commodify everything that is culture

when the vampire stands outside, witnessing a heart-wrenchingly beautiful musical performance that ends up harmonising with everything that is divine in this godless world, there is this loathe and disgust in his eyes. this desire to capture. this desire to make it their own. as is with every art form and culture hitherto. everyone seeks to appropriate, approximate and package - to reduce the value of it all; to detach the art from the artist; to extinguish the fire it causes amongst people, the voice it gives to people, the empathy it provides them and a collective form of rebellion it is towards the power that be. it scares them. 

long live art! <3

caught this on a flight back to india after a long day and i am not disappointed in the slightest 

i don’t know why i put off watching for the longest time (maybe because of the ugly poster?) but stree is an incredibly fun genre film that wraps itself and it’s crux in this neat social satire while not getting didactic for a second and also balancing the tight rope between satire which is as subtle as the b in subtle and as abrasive as a bus plowing you down

written by raj and dk, and directed by amar kaushik - this has a lot to offer and it offers one thing consistently which is a shit loads of fun

“wo stree hai, purush nahi”

honour killings, pent up sexual frustrations being taken out on women is things all so common in india - rural india all that much more. don’t step out of your home at night, make sure you wear these type of clothes, make sure you don’t respond to aggravation, make sure to not face them or fight back. flipping the rhetorics on their head while simultaneously ensuring they fit the narrative is done so swiftly with the makers and it’s so rewarding to watch. 

there are few gripes i have with the film, the first being the soundtrack having the most horrendous generic songs. secondly, i wish there was more of an ernest attempt at horror - bhool bhulaiyaa being the most relevant example of achieving that balance, it’s incredible, noone has dethroned it so far. 

despite these, a film for the ages, no wonder this outsold animal.

quite literally the quintessential patriotic desi cinema film than a thousand akshay kumar fauji thrillers combined

superboys of malegaon is a film that wears its heart on its sleeves and just as you reciprocate that heartfelt gesture - it stomps on it mercilessly until it stiches it back together in one big swift move

there is not a single beat wasted, not a single character’s weight ever miscalculated - this also feels a bit heavy sometimes causing whiplash with the sudden new bgms and scene progression, however, i digress

the film is in constant dialogue with the art form and the makers of the said art. a cautionary tale for the directors and the writers alike and the end “lesson” being being empathetic. i put lessons in quotes because the film isn’t didactic in the things it wants to say. there is this simultaneous celebration of cinema as is the sprinkled critique of the larger capitalist industry that wraps this cinema of ours - and often abstracts it to the point of losing machli ki aankh type focus on what actually matters in cinema - people

people of all walks, all kinds. everyone deserves to be seen and everyone’s story deserves to be told. and to the naysayers, who would pout and dismiss the need for such voices, the film points to deewar, a story of a mill worker. 

the writer and the director need each other as much as they need every single person involved in the making - grover saab having been both quite a few times feels deeply about this and it is quite apparent in the writing. films on films are so wonderful hamesha!

the film’s most charming quality remains in how it begins to wrap up towards the end, the way it beautifully converge with the real life events a lot of us would be familiar with from supermen of malegaon and ends with a beautiful reminder of the very real people who’s story we finally got to hear (and makes you bawl kinda ngl)

incredible piece of cinema!

also shoutout to the teenager next to me who asked his friend during the film “ye javed akhtar kaun hai?” and his friend replied with “writer hai shaayad, dekhte hai baad mai”. jo in logo ka dimaag fattne waala hai ghar jaake maa kasam

i like to think of it as a reflective inverted mirror of after hours

while in after hours, there is this sense of comfort in the characters interacting while the city has this je na sa qui dissonance and anxiety to it

this film has this incredibly alluring milieu and world filled with jazz and neon lit streets, the characters are the dissonant anxiety-inducing sad cogs of this machine

the people are debauchery filled crazy ass people who go around doing as they wish as if they were the absurd man camus keeps talking about

the film moves at a pace so smooth that if you notice closely, you end up doing a smooth dolly towards the screen during the runtime of the film

the characters are screwballs as they are supposed to be, they are supposed to be people who you look at and go huh what a bunch of fucking lunatics and the film earnestly doesn't just show us the screwballs and romanticize every screw up they do, it rather dips us in this giant river of despair to really hammer up the consequences of these screwbally life - so much so that, there is no respite for most, there is a brief moment of respite for 2 of them out of the 10 - which respite as we are sure by now won't last all that long

“man proposes, god disposes”

another innovative film that has long been lost with piss poor archiving efforts and neglect - once more i had to create the letterboxd page and add its information online but anyway, on with the review

call girl is a film that is interestingly a classic bollywood film with tons of musicals and melodrama yet its heart, plot turns and cinematography scream “parallel”

focusing on maya aka kamini who is a call girl (a sex worker) who is played beautifully by zaheera. its her story as is evident by the incredibly pretty poster. 

"so tum kaunsi business branch join karoge? yahaan ki ya national?"
"mai paint karna chahta hu"
"paint yahaan par? humne abhi to paint karaaya hai idhar office mai"
"aap galat samjhe. artist."
"artist? idiot"

amar is a rich privileged kid who was in america for ages to study for his degree but comes back utterly infatuated with art and starts courting kamini. saying all tall things about his undying love and proclaiming her to be the height of all that is divine. this is all ofcourse until he founds out that she is a sex worker, thats when he flips out. foregoing every bit of endearment and love he initially felt just as the thought of the woman not being “pure” crossed his mind. there is this incredible scene where in during the revelation/confrontation, the phone keeps ringing loudly amidst the chaos and noise of them fighting with each other; the phone through which maya usually conducts her business as amar flips over her life and work - it’s really fucking good. 

the film also doesn’t make her be some damsel in distress waiting to be saved

"apni marzi se shareer bechti thi, and ab apni marzi se nahi bechungi"

and to top the whole film off, there is this incredibly dramatic dialogue of sonachand with himself as the film transforms into this nightmarish hellscape and the incompetent amar has to live his life with these consequences as do all the other rotten men in the film

beautifully shot, too!

an incredibly fascinating piece of film history that also happens to be an incredible film which was also nominated for the golden palm at cannes! (and snubbed imo)

written and directed by khwaja ahmad abbas and vasili pronin - a unique indian-soviet collaboration film. before anything about that or the film, i want to spend some time expressing my regret and sadness over the lack of respect we dispel over the great mr. abbas. he needs to be revered much more and much wider - it’s an upsetting situation wherein even the most geekiest of cinephiles will gladly skim over one of the greatest filmmakers to ever live. mr. abbas apart from this film, has written neecha nagar which is another fantastic film, he also written and directed dharti ke lal. several documentaries and also several literary publishings. a man who deserves to be revered and to any reader who stumbles upon this review, please check out khwaja ahmad abbas and his work. now onto the film!

this film as aforementioned is a unique film that has an incredibly intricate meta layer of commentary where in the film is about a russian trader who comes to india specifically to trade and falls in love with the culture, the people and nargis (who really wouldn’t fall in love with nargis). why is it meta is because this was made during the peak of indo-soviet relations and this film was coproduced with the soviet state film fund. its an incredibly genius move to adapt the travelogue into this film which is somehow not only an entertaining and insightful period piece but also an apt representation of the current relations the two nations foster

the film has some incredible compositions and the runtime is brisk and breezes through. the musical numbers are so well shot - even though alas, we haven’t preserved this film as well as we should have. 

at its core, its a celebration of india’s spirit and a story about a traveller who is drawn to adventure even if means risking everything else. the spirit of india runs deep in hospitality and kindness - in enthusiasm and compassion - in acceptance and diversity - and this is how you have a “muslim director” doing a beautiful ramayan narration midway through while the lyrics “ye hindustan hai pyaare, humaari jaan hai pyaare” are sung passionately into your ears

absolute cinema and if my partner doesn’t start dancing like nargis urging me not to leave, is it really even love?

neecha nagar, based on the lower depths by maxim gorky - with thematic resemblance to fritz lang's metropolis is a film that was also the first indian film to win the palme d'or (then called grand prix)

the main conflict lies in this scenario where there are a bunch of capitalists who have this waste they want to dispose of from their posh bourgeoisie area to the poor area's river. they want to make this happen as it's convenient and well the other people? they are poor ofc so a lot of them would buy into this pipe dream of them also getting some of this luxury and inexplicably escaping from the depths. this is how the capitalist overlord ensures that no real resistance is formed - ensuing distrust amongst the very people hoping to stop him. oh and the film also has something similar, i wasn’t really talking about the film yet

the film is very beautifully lit and shot with people carrying fire torches in their hands as they unite in massive numbers looking like an abstract art piece to crows circling over the god forsaken place

the great ravi shankar scores the entire film with some great tracks and dance sequence dispersed in between (though a lot of it was scrapped when the film was sent to cannes)

“tum meri kutpatli ho, mai tumhaara annadaata hu” (you guys are my puppets and me your provider) is said by the overlord when the people propose an alternative

a wonderful film with the messages that still ring true to this very day. even more so now, seeing the country being systematically sold to the overlords with the people living in the neecha nagar once again seeing their polluted drains be the norm

it’s baffling to me that we stopped making films that would challenge the status quo so openly. which would beg the question of stopping them in time. which would portray these megalomaniac villains (a lot of times, amrish puri if we fast forward a few decades) succumbing to their own greed of wealth. i guess, a lot of sigma motivation and phonk music has really deteriorated anything resembling social realism

an eclectic yet calm piece about birds, delhi and india

the family of wildlife rescuers act as a vessel to bring upon light onto india, delhi and everything befalling the aforementioned

the documentary is so meticulously filmed that it feels like a full feature film with the clever editing telling a full fledged narrative

though, it's the very fact that it's not one, that it's not a fictional film that makes everything hit harder. this is about the very real people doing very real things in a city that has been left to decay - words that are even truer considering what we are seeing recently

the film is also profound and the profoundness coming from our incredibly intelligent protagonists and their actions

"humans often forget they are just lump of meats"

we often do, placing too much value on us and our petty overarching conflicts as is the case when humans try to inflict pain onto other humans based on their identity. often forgetting that

"duniya khud ek tarah ki biradri hai, hum hawa se jude hua hai" (trns. humans are a family of their own, connected by the air)

leaving us with the hateful landscape we see today in real time with people not being allowed to leave their homes to vote. people being threatened to shoot by the police if they dare leave their houses to vote because

"hum pehle bhi dange dekhe hai. lekin, is baar sirf nafrat nahi hai, chaaro taraf ghin hai" (trns. we have seen riots before but this time it's not just hatred - there is disgust everywhere)

incredible work by everyone involved in the film and to really hammer home the care put on this film, the credits are as beautiful as the entire film

awara is a film so refreshing while not being very unique in its plot. even though its not unique in its plot, there are some things it says which are also not unique but the way the film says it is what makes it excellent 

there are so many working wheels spinning at the same time saying one thing or the other and raj kapoor carries it all with such incredible charm. the best actor and filmmaker of the kapoor family from a long mile. raj kapoor fighting with himself is one of the most charming scenes i have ever seen

several film making techniques are employed to deliver very expressionist surreal imagery reminiscent of fritz lang and welles

there are a lot of things film sets out to critique like for example the sequence where the young leela is being thrown out after jagga made her “impure” being conveyed with dialogues like 

“sita ko bhi agni pariksha deni padi thi…

stree ki laaj ka shisha tut jaaye to phir kabhi nahi jud sakta…

aurat ki jaat hi bewafa hoti hai”

or 

“these capitalists - if you wear a fancy suit you are not thought to be a thief. ye punjiwaadi…”

or

“choro ko nahi rakhna chahte taaki wo hamesha chori se apna pet bharein?” (if you don’t hire convicts, do you always want them to just be thieves?)

the film has these things to be said and more where it critiques social norms, deep rooted patriarchy, rehabilitation and the prison complex. all of it culminating in an incredible court drama where in a very didactic manner we are implored to think about our society and its functionings.

now i understand why this film was one of the favourites of mr. mao

expected a more nuanced take but remains to be just as bit one dimensional and banal as the counterpart indian nationalistic drivel that india produces (though now supporting the “founding father” of india is an unpopular opinion in India haha)

the film has nothing more to say than what would be known by just about everyone - possibly because except for the history textbooks we have all read, they didn’t have anything else to go with. yet, somehow the film insists on making nehru into a caricature idiot who is just an insecure old man against the “great yet calm stature of jinnah” is what the film says repeatedly into your ears. cringe worthy sequences [sometimes wrapped in the dreamy flashback excuse of it all being a dreamesque sequence - which I will get to] of mr jinnah coincidentally standing outside doors eavesdropping on conversations about him oh wow! gandhi says that jinnah will call him “a wily old man” and he does in a later scene!! oh wow guys.

i absolutely dislike the "dead jinnah looking back at his life time through time travel" plot device because it often makes serious moments of his life feel like caricature because of how poorly the moments are explored. just having jinnah go "oh nooo don't do that noo" as she dies is not a profound statement

the film has a few monologues where just the fact that some of jinnah’s ideas are verbatim able to be translated on the screen by lee’s gravitas aiding it give rise to some powerful moments

but all of that is not enough to protect the fall of everything else. there is a scene in between which tries to show an adult jinnah flirting with a 16 year old rattanbai jinnah. that was a different time with varying understanding of marriageable age and consent but holy shit lol retrospectively showing that as a positive is a choice for sure.

christopher lee delivers a great performance but choosing english as the primary language for a film based on the indo-pakistan conflict bogs down the film the most. hindi-urdu would have been obviously a natural fit - even more so because this anglicization of the whole matter is ironic

before playing the film, dibakar said “a film is not a film until people see it” and for this film its more true than any other film because of the positive impact it will have on a lot of people if it reaches them

tees is an excellent film with so much to say yet it never feels overwhelming. there are 3 separate timelines and stories told interjecting each other and as easy it was for it to get convoluted, it doesn’t for even a second

“aag zyaada der tak na dekhein to uska darr khatam ho jaata hai”

the cycle of generations, the identity passed down from generations and the baggage alongside of it. unchecked laissez-faire capitalism and authoritarian government rule leading to a living condition so deplorable, so unfair. yet, amidst all this, amidst this hopelessness, amidst the tragic events in its backdrop, there is this hopefulness that permeates through and its beautiful

dibakars best, indian cinema working at its best. huma qureshi, zoya hussein, shashank arora, nasser sahab and everyone giving an incredible performance and yet noone can see it. 

the film also in a twisted fate of irony plays semi autobiographically with netflix staying its release

and lastly,
i asked dibakar after the film “if established filmmakers like you and anurag are unable to make the films that you want. what hope do independent filmmakers like us have?”

to which dibakar replied “it’s gonna get a lot worse before it gets better. some of us won’t even be here after it, a lot of us will be extinguished. being honest with you, its a lot tougher for you to start than it was for me when i started making films. you will have to fight through. a tough fight but ladna padega”

this is a film teetering tottering between being an anti film and being a shocking superhero film - this is the film’s most charming quality 

its not until the very end that you realize that it is one of the two

todd philips finds himself in a weird spot after the unprecedented success of the first one (i dont like the first one as much since king of comedy is just that much better)

the direction todd takes this in is very interesting and appreciable where instead of being a cashgrab with another sequel in the bag to milk the absolute fuck out of the formula that unexpectedly worked so well for the first film (cough, hangover) - todd wants a send off. and he wants a send off which is bound to piss off so many people. its not satisfying. it doesnt have the overly stylized violence, it doesnt have *that* monologue which will be posted by sigmas because we live in a society. the film intentionally subverts all the established tropes to leave you utterly disappointed to the point of wondering what this film really is? 

the film is a super stylish and technically impressive anti film which works if you are in on the meta commentary of a comic book movie signing off on artistic choices because the first one worked unexpectedly while the director intentionally wants to instead “focus on emotions” which falls flat because its a superhero film with a comic book character who says stuff like we live in a society. yet, because todd wanted to piss off the fans, he does just that. it's a fuck you screamed to the incels who were parading the first film and diminishing what he had, in his own convoluted way, wanted to say

btw, shoutout to the dude in front of me who googled “why is joker singing” 6 times during the runtime at different places. ending the searches saga with “why is joker singing in the end?”

this is like a 14 year old edge lord on the internet got to make a film

the film starts with “2000 A.D. Bastar” to show the tribals living in primitive conditions and then fast forwards decades to show how there’s been no development because that what this film is. thats the lack of nuance this whole film carries throughout its runtime. 

“oh look the evil communists just want to kill people but hey the government is also corrupt!” is screamt at you in the first 20 minutes but you obviously know its the communists who are corrupt as the film shows them to be these horrendous people who lurk in the shadows recruiting people😼

“twitter lame hai bro, no bro facebook is lame, twitter is cool” - is an actual dialogue written 

this film also is very clear in their stance on women. “oh look bro stupid campaign against vigilantism against women and moral policing -  done by hollow people who have no moral sense in actuality”

the film is a pain to go through and i have a headache having gone through it. its vivek agnihotri screaming "hey guys do you know all protest and dissent is fake and actually terrorism?” at you for 2 hours

bombay velvet should be taught in film schools not because its a great film but its a lesson in how compromising your voice and original intentions at every point can lead to a shitty product that will benefit neither you or the people asking you to compromise

this film will always be so interesting to me especially because of anurag’s original vision. he wanted to make a trilogy exploring how mumbai came to be. exploring the depths from which capitalism and the influential people shaped it into being - from force or other ways. just the premise is so fascinating and seeing it explored in a trilogy wouldve been a sight

alas, we didn’t get that. we got something else. and what we got is a film that is just nothing?

the film is constantly in a hurry to jump from one thing to the next, do this and then do that next, oh no lets not pause, cut, omg you get the point move on, now this, now exposition, now info dump - its all so fucking exhausting to sit through

and yet, why is that? has anurag lost his craft? he has told several times that on the edit table the producers were involved in minutely cutting the script, cutting the scenes because they wanted the film to have a “broader appeal”. Thelma Schoonmaker was responsible for the majority of the editing so it’s not obviously her who did a sloppy job - its the extra editing that was imposed on it.

the sets while lavish lack character? the characters while interesting are never developed. the mumbai story barely glossed over with a big focus on avoiding any controversy by resemblance of anyone real even slightly

compromise, greed and a lack of autonomy gives us a film like bombay velvet marking it as a film which could’ve been so much but wasn’t able to

and its sad because there is some really good stuff scattered around. there is anurag’s attention to detail with anushka sharma coming out of goa for the first time being stopped by Portuguese soldiers because goa was portugal’s enclave for a while post independence or how there are character moments which are pure homage to great films or how the soundtrack is so well produced

it’s a film that leaves you sad that I don’t recommend you watch except for a meta analysis

tumbbad is a film which somehow strikes the perfect balance between being a genuinely spooky horror film while still delivering the statement it wants to deliver without sacrificing the elements of the former

a film which took close to 6 years to finish, with the makers opting to shoot at real locations with minimal CG - the result is that much more appealing to look at

greed and men - that's what fuels the film and that's what it wants to err you against. greed and male chauvinism are the real horror elements in the film. there is a sequence of scenes where:

pandurang learning from dad - offers a gold mudra to vinayak's mistress. pandurang's smirk as he offers the mudra to the mistress is enough to send chills down your spine.

following that, there is a scene between vinayak and pandurang where vinayak is beating pandurang for what he did and bursts out laughing manically when he sees the mirrored greed in pandurang, the mirrored chauvinism, the "haraamipana". incredible scene - acted and crafted to perfection

there are so many more nods, metaphors and subtle details that are a delight to see

the fact that the recreated city has original posters of alam ara in the background for more historical accuracy. the fact that vinayak's wife while he is gone starts selling food to the city under the banner of "brahmini ke haath ka shudh khaana". the fact that the whole film is allegorically referring to a brahmin exploiting the gods for money

my favourite of it all being that the implication that because of the god's curse - because of man's greed - tumbbad being perpetually cursed with rain. the implication that mumbai is another such place perpetually cursed with rain because of the greed of people

as everyone who knows me is aware, i avoid looking at even a slither of information about any film i am going to watch to have the rawest, unadulterated experience possible - not contaminated by a single outside opinion or word

the routine was done with this film and yet there was this confusion throughout the majority of the runtime I had about what is this film trying to say. every film wants to say something - what was this film’s intentions? while I was delighted by the incredible performances by pankaj kapur and shabana azmi - this thought crept up several times. is it about the relationship between dibankar and his wife? is it a cool fictional discovery fairy tale? is it an examination of the broken bureaucracy of our country holding us down hitherto? the last one seemed to be the theme and was solidified for me in the second half and yet there were moments where I thought that the film is a little hamfisted because while I am aware of the bureaucracy having dealt with it first hand, surely these caricatures is an exaggeration. there seems to be no reason for them to act this way surely? as the film ended on a lighter note, i was ready to close mubi only to be flashed by the ending credits claiming “based on a true incident”. learning the film is based on the life of dr subhash mukhopahdyay broke my heart and simultaneously made me appreciate the film so much more

the film changes the subject of research and fictionalises the doctors and corresponding places but somehow is able to give such a stark yet accurate portrayal of dr subash. from the birth of the invention being in this dingy homemade lab to the expert committee being comprised of people from non-related fields. tapan sinha is able to gather the closest historic count of the incident and extrapolate it to deliver a compelling story even without knowing the background behind it. 

mr sinha also does another thing which cements this film as a great film where he chooses to give the fictional dr subash a happy ending, an ending where he is appreciated albeit not by his kinfolk but rather people outside his country barring the fictional dibankar roy from the fate of dr subash who committed suicide leaving behind a note reading “i can’t wait everyday for a heart attack to kill me”

few, few films ever come close to achieving what this film achieves. naturalist realism poignant melodrama with a big mirror held up to the political state of india - incredible

showcasing kanpur in its absolute rawness - highlighting the life that many lead day in and day out. a city (alike many others) severely mismanaged and neglected forcing this not so well oiled machine to be constructed where two wheels go grinding on each other with tons of friction and in erratic steps with one of the wheels being the bureaucrats, a lot of them often well meaning, failing to make any significant change and the other wheel being the powers that be with their usual snake oil salesman tactics. the wheels often being connected to bigger machineries with bigger parts as you pull farther away from it, with more levels of abstraction, and more and more encapsulation and abstractions that it's impossible to point at one part of the machine and try to fix that part. the vast spreading machine is confusing and inconsistent with the only commonality being the the regular resident of the city gets grinded to dust in the middle of the wheels and the several parts

a good reminder for us to also not be myopic and remember the vast neglect that carries on from different regimes.

great privilege check which is also beautifully made, beautifully edited, and beautifully shot - reminded me of my village and it's power outages where I would literally sit for hours on end actually praying to the gods to bring us some electricity lol

this is a very interesting film who's lore is also an important part of indian cinema. never officially screened in india due to disputes with the censor board (wow, I have never heard about this happening here) - leaving obscurely placed copies available online with a brief stint on mubi, too

the film itself is unique in the way that it utilises mumbai and it's many vivid landscapes to bring character to the plot in a very edward hopper wim wender esque way

the film wants to say a lot, A LOT - that is indeed a bit confusing with characters sometimes acting borderline schizophrenic to move the plot in the way intended; and honestly, that's not really a complaint. amidst the thousands of films with not a lot to say, atleast this film has something to say even if it is a lot

the film also parallels saeed akhtar mirza's albert pinto very closely but transforming it into this neo noir cutting chai of a film - though, I reckon (as another review I saw pointed out) that it is not didactic enough for that haha

some characters are interesting, with tannishtha chatterjee's mona being the most interesting and 3 dimensional. nishikant kamat also delivers a great performance even if his character can sometimes feel restrictive with only expositions and volitions tailored to the plot's ultimate point

the tv as a motif is also very well executed with chabia and mona's sequence in bed being my favourite

an interesting watch which has a lot to say with some great quotables in between that resonates themes frequent in mrinal sen's work and la haine in particular acting as a big inspiration

and lastly, my favourite trope in indian art house films is people watching anil kapoor films inside the film

patriarchy is often talked about in the zeitgeist these days and that's great because we do need more conversations about patriarchy and the faux image of masculinity alongside of it; however there are times where the aforementioned aren't loud and abrasive or rather not easily definable

what does it mean to be a man? is it having a lot of sex with lots of women while maintaining that you're very potent or drinking whiskey on the rocks instead of cocktails or smoking red cigarettes instead of vaping or working in STEM-adjacent fields while maintaining a distance from the arts?

"be a man" or rather mockingly "ladki hai kya?" are often things paraded around at the slightest showing of the tiniest amount of emotional intelligence

there is this unique intersection when masculinity collides with financial conditions - ironically, creating a cocktail of the ultimate disassociation. it's not just that you shouldn't do these things but rather now you can't in good conscience for if you falter or fail, you don't have any larger means to fall down on. for if things don't work out, you will be harshly impacting not only you but the people who provide for you

there is something very harrowing and very uncomfortable about seeing a family escape from north korea in realtime as they hop from borders, evade the police and are in genuine unadulterated terror - so much so that sometimes the film borders on exploitation more than exploration but I think it firms stays in the realm of the latter 

i have lived in south korea for 3 months or so for a project, and whenever I would talk to the people I was working with about north korea, there was a solemn sigh and usually a statement around how the people are being mistreated - so sympathy towards them. i found that very interesting, because the general sentiment in my home country runs rampantly hate filled towards people from a similarly separated country, similar language spoken, similar looking people, similarly sponsored by the two global superpowers

while yes obviously the above is a not so informed anecdotal observation, I highlight it to really illustrate how much care is given and the resources that are spent by the south to help the people living under that megalomaniac regime. and obviously, its not all roses either, and general discrimination against NK immigrants does exist in the country but what really stands out is the general acceptance, the general care for the people they consider their own despite tall orchestrated borders, despite geopolitical strategies trying to pull them apart 

this is an excellent documentary that is a very uncomfortable watch and rightfully so. the life threatening process they have to undergo to escape the country is trumped by the hardships they have to face in their daily life. they have to risk their lives, risk the lives of their loved ones, just so they can have a slight chance at having a life where they can be well fed. that’s all they really want. as for the one scene that will live with me forever, the grandma having escaped and being asked about her views on kim jong-un to which she earnestly replies despite being prompted several times to not lie and that it’s okay - her earnest genuine reply being something along the lines of “he is a great marshal and a great leader. if only we people worked harder, if we didn’t let him down, we might have running water 247 and food”

there's a certain charm that booksmart wears underneath its sleeve that makes the whole film all that more entertaining

in films, sometimes the messaging gets botched because of caricatures while in other cases, sometimes the actual story gets botched because of the messaging but this film achieves a great balance in between

teenage is a tough time. body-image issues, big career shifts, uncertainty about the future, letting go of familiar relationships and people. we are often compartmentalised into separate categories when we are teenagers - nerd but smart, jock but loser. booksmart tries bridging the gap between these two with a superbad esque comedy stringing it all together.

the film relies on teenage comedy tropes a lot intentionally just so it can subvert the tropes to reveal other facets to these otherwise caricature characters

it's a fun film to watch with a killer soundtrack ranging from death grips, rtj, dj shadow to salt n pepa and jurassic 5 - with all the music being composed by dan the automator. it was going to be a good movie.

there is something about the milieu constructed by kieslowski that leaves this ingrained sense of having lived in his films - the atmosphere he portrays is so thick that you could smoothly pierce through with a butter knife revealing the several layers beneath

so, let's talk about the several layers beneath. “thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain” is the commandment that kieslowski decides to explore through this part of decalogue and alike the first one, he is able to give such a contemporary intriguing interpretation of it that it’s a delight to go through

the taking of God’s name is interpreted as protecting the sanctity of speech, of giving someone your word, of swearing to someone

unlike the first part of dekalog, there is not a biblical devastating tragedy as the result of the failure to comply to the commandment but rather kieslowski is much more interested in portraying a more grounded outcome - a tragedy which is hurtful but which is realistic none the less - a tragedy which could very well happen to anyone in our modern world

lying is fundamentally wrong and more so if you convince yourselves that the lie is being told for the “greater good” or that it could potentially “save” a life - playing god to prevent other people’s hypothetical sufferings just because you have suffered a great loss

just like the film, i can’t find a definitive way to end this review like I usually do but hey sometimes the endings leave you wondering and with more thoughts than before ;)

parallel cinema of india pre-y2k has always drawn from the french new wave a lot while also giving this very unique cultural spin on it all. sen, benegal, saeed mirza, gulzar, ghatak, dutt, ray, nihalani, aravindan, ketan mehta, bimal roy - all have these innate distinct niches that make their work absolutely pop out at once amongst the sea of great parallel works. i have always disliked the term "parallel cinema" since it attaches this compartmentalization connotation to it that bogs down what the films are - they are not just art-house flicks aimed at the elite snooty folks but rather films meant to be experienced by everyone and ones which will connect with everyone and i think mandi is one of many such great examples

mandi is a film that functions as a satirical comedy at places and at times becomes an exploration of capitalism and aristocrats failing to understand the humanity that flourishes in businesses that fall outside their moral umbrella. rukmani bai runs a brothel housing several women, many of whom she has brought up since the time they were children. the brothel acts as a safe haven for all the women who have been exploited, kidnapped, trafficked, sold off and provides them dignity

benegal doesn't portray their work as a sob story for even a second and that's the greatest strength of this film. there is this innate empathy and humanity sprinkled all across every character in this film. this isn't the regular tragedy porn you would expect from a film about sex work. all the workers are content with their work while also not denying the massive exploitation they experience. every one exhibits this incredible bravery and love for the arts - qualities that are the least associated with sex workers in the usual portrayals of the same in our zeitgeist

the men in this film range from either greedy businessmen, snake oil salesmen or a submissive partner to the women and that's something that makes the whole film even more delightful. the film is about women. powerful women doing their best to survive in a world with odds so overtly stacked against them with an additional caveat of their work being considered "immoral" attracting further scrutiny from everyone including other women in the guise of them wanting to help these "poor women"

the film is also so incredibly shot with some shots looking impossibly curated

this might be my favorite performance from amrish puri and shabana azmi - and that is saying A LOT considering the sheer strength of their filmography

i cant ever see om puri ji as a pervert photographer though, my heart would never allow that. benegal sir aisa kyu kiye aap 🙏

the biggest disservice done to jaggi has been it being paraded by non-intersectional queer pages of india as a “rural queer exploration film”. while there are queer elements in the film based in rural northern india (and I would love to see a film exploring these elements in detail), these elements are very much not the focus of exploration of jaggi and labelling it as so hugely undermines and misguides what the film is able to achieve. 

life in rural india is weird and not really something that could be easily defined, explained or portrayed. there are many intricacies in how people behave, how people react and what ripple impact it usually causes en masse. 

sex. it’s something that inherently is a taboo for everyone in India. the extent to which varies in India with some urban areas having larger acceptance and progressiveness about it to rural settings having a more orthodox view on it. but never the less, it’s not that the less progressive places don’t want to have sexual intimacy or that, to them sexual attachment is not natural. 

natural. it’s natural to want to be intimate as it is natural to have an orientation pertaining to partners. you don’t choose who you’re attracted to. it’s natural to be attracted to a certain group of people. 

but what happens when sex and attraction is not dictated by nature but rather governed by this closely knitted society rampant with toxic masculinity and outside the vacuum of which, not much exists, we get what happens to jaggi

absolutely dominated with this toxic masculinity, every thought not inline with it is absolutely shunned and ostracised. every thing whether that be general asexuality or a medical problem preventing sex or homosexuality are all elements that are consistently thrown out of society. 

children from a very young age go through this process of separation with the concerns of not “being a man” dominating their world sphere until the day they die. 

and the honest to god exploration of it is why the movie is one of the finest movies of this generation. jaggi paints this realistic world in such a grim real way that it’s hard to take your eyes off for a second. it explores sexual frustration leading to a normalisation of sexual assault. it explores how villages really end up damaging an individual and how trapped they end up feeling. it explores trauma and it’s deep rooted impact. it explores the general lack of empathy and understanding towards sexuality due to the extreme taboo nature of the same all while delivering a story that is sure to shake you to your core. and a story that anyone from a village, myself included, will be forced to introspect and gain new perspectives that might have been forgotten in the gradual process “upliftment” and gentrification - also highlighting the need to deliver such stories so a newer generation might be impacted and spared of the same abuse. absolute cinema. 

also, the ending of it absolutely resembling my short film was so surreal to see. i will just pretend that siddhu ji saw my film and was inspired. (its not true and noone will believe me)

twin peaks is a crime drama with a supernatural setting on the surface but the show represents something more personal and deeper about lynch/frost and their outlook on life and art

the show is a staunch statement on the state of art. on the state of how we interact with art and what art truly means

i recognize the words im saying seem to be very dramatic but bear with me for a second, we will get to what it means

i have dissected the themes of twin peaks as a whole and the different things it means to me on my review of fire walk with me. this is an extension of the same.

twin peaks: the return taking place 25 years after twin peaks jumps us into a world so modern that it's honestly jarring.

while twin peaks feels like this compact chocolate cake with multiple layers beneath it that are revealed slowly as you go through it and realize that the chocolate is actually hard charred blood and bones infused with charcoal at the heart of it instead of the deliciousness we expected
twin peaks the return instead feels like this massive scary pool of ingredients scattered around which all resemble the visuals of blood and gore until we finally realize at the bottom of it lies a delicious cherry pie dessert once we actually break through the scary exterior

while, the first two seasons are defined by our highly likeable protagonist dale cooper. return is defined by the lack of our beloved and the show really makes you yearn for it.

it's a bold decision to turn your most likeable character into the most disgusting hunk as we yearn for the person we love to come back. as we dougie jones frolic around, get out of situations through this divine protection he carries around him despite not being 'awake'. it's a relationship you really begin to miss and lynch is fully aware of this.

episode by episode, bit by bit, you miss him, you yearn for him and the show produces this palpable anxiety as everyone relevant tries to string together the pieces slowly, bit by bit, in a way where it's almost frustrating but the show does it slowly and that's what I want to talk about next

the show is in itself a rebellious act against the very constructs of how our beloved movie/tv industry works. the show is a clear staunch fuck you to the structures/paradigms that every show or movie finds itself having to adhere to. the show has consistent commentary between old vs new - not just in the actual content as apparent through dr. jacoby's entertaining monologues but rather through the show's structure and the way it circumvents every possible convention.

the original twin peaks was a show relying on familiar crime/horror tropes to dazzle us with a unique milieu around the show with some deep spiritual elements - delivering a solid modernist masterpiece. the return on the other hands borrows from the post-modernist structure/editing to an extent and then runs away from it as soon it begins boxing the show into a definable entity.

from the show's opening titles not having cold opens to the show's ending, all culminate in this act of not conforming to established traditions. the way that every episode ends is alone a statement on what this show wants to be seen as. instead of a cliffhanger or an enticing plot line, every episode ends with this a live musical performance from some very talented artists at the bar, from nine inch nails to pearl jam to julee cruise, they sing and it's beautifully shot. they sing and it's calming and soothing as the credits slowly roll in. instead of trying to optimize every aspect of the show so as to not avoid losing people's interest for even a second, the show instead beckons you to be patient, beckons you to take it all in.

we are increasingly in the age of conformity in art. almost every fashion icon converge in the way they look. almost every film is structured in a way that resemble each others with auteurs becoming even more rare as we go further. this show is an oasis amongst the desert that is cinema sometimes.

from the way the special effects are used and the way characters behave, it hides a certain genuinity beneath it all. the ending has a scene where a floating 2D ball is trying to attack a kid with a glove and it's actually terrifying to go through. it's a show which has made a tea kettle seem menacing. it's a show which tries to inspire, which tries to pack spirituality into a modern crime drama, which says fuck you to transphobia, which critiques our increasingly consumerist society

through all this is how you're able to make a person waking up from his bed and say "i'm the FBI" some of the most emotionally packed cathartic moments in the history television

and finally, this is why after the penultimate ending episode which almost seems like a warm hug eventually throws you out on the road with the actual ending so that you can wonder, so that you can speculate, so that your imagination keeps running and so that you remember to explore and not be okay with conformity

thank you mr frost and mr lynch

fernandes is a man who is just going through the motions ever since the love of his life died. he works on autopilot - suspending any sense of grip he had on life when his loved ones were alive.

ila is a wife trapped in a patriarchal marriage with an unavailable husband who has hope. she tries, in stark contrast to fernandes. ila isn't complacent and would not be despite of what atrocity befalls her.

shaikh is an orphan who has had noone in his life ever since he was a child. he has had noone to rely on and yet continues to storm through a life with a grit not familiar to fernandes or ila.

the incidental connection between ila and fernandes shines as a ray of hope for both of them. the letters are convenient and abstract away the metrics associated with life. alike how the ink on paper eventually withers away, so would their fantasy pen pal world.

fernandes understands his age, and understands the consequences of his age. he is old and gets old every day. while ila has a long healthy life in front of her. fernandes, as he usually does, has this sacrificial quality to him where he absolutely feels a future for him isn't destined and retiring away from the place he knows and loves is the fate he deserves.

ila, retains the optimism she starts with of making this incredibly unique connection possible that might lead to the betterment of both of their lives.

shaikh deeply bonds with fernandes and sees the father figure he didn't have growing up in fernandes. fernandes fills up a void in shaikh's life that he never truly internalized he ever had. shaikh too gains this optimism about a future not so bleak.

this optimism while greatly convenient is one that lacks much rationale behind it. these relationships and connections while very pure are also very brittle and would break into unhappy concoctions if tested.

ila, slowly realizes, that her fate would be of the two women she loves in her life. her upstairs neighbor and her mom. she too would be stuck in a loop of taking care of a man significantly older than him when the time does unfortunately befall upon to do so. while, she would have probably scoffed this concern off, seeing her mother relieved at the death of her father instills this deeply in her that despite the sheer servitude and devotion to a person you love, you would end up in the place that fernandes is. a person going through the motions because their loved one was lost.

shaikh realizes that while the bond is real and there is genuine love between them. this is but a temporary affair and the void would be retained once the month is over and the responsibilities are once again literally and figuratively shifted back to him.

and through all this, fernandes realizes that there is no metric that is universal. there are no rules that are universal. and the only way to grieve isn't to be a bitter old man living in nashik waiting for his final days to come. that there is life left, however much the quantity, there is life left.
